--- title: "[Family]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-abc}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Abstract family defining the response distribution and link function. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L14-L318){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python Family() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} A `Family` encapsulates everything the P-IRLS fitting loop needs to know about the conditional distribution of the response `y` given the linear predictor `eta`. Every GLM and GAM family in Whittaker belongs to the exponential dispersion family, and is fully characterized by three ingredients: 1. The **link function** `g`, relating the mean `mu` to the linear predictor `eta`: `eta = g(mu)`, along with its inverse and derivative. 2. The **variance function** `V(mu)`, relating the variance of the response to its mean: `Var(Y) = phi * V(mu)`, where `phi` is the dispersion (scale) parameter. 3. The **deviance** and **log-likelihood**, which quantify goodness of fit and are used by `GAM.fit()` for smoothing parameter selection (GCV/REML) and by `GAM.summary()` for reporting. Subclasses must implement all abstract methods (`link`, `link_inverse`, `link_derivative`, `variance`, `deviance`, `log_likelihood`, `simulate`). The link function and its inverse/derivative are used by the P-IRLS algorithm to form pseudo-data (the working response `z`) and working weights `W` at each iteration. Families whose loss does not fit the standard GLM deviance framework (e.g. `QuantileFamily`, `CoxPH`, `OrderedCategorical`, `Multinomial`) may instead override `irls_update` to supply `z` and `W` directly. Whittaker ships with the following concrete families: - `Gaussian` — identity link, constant variance; the default family for continuous, unbounded responses. - `Poisson` — log link, `V(mu) = mu`; for count data. - `Binomial` — logit link, `V(mu) = mu(1-mu)`; for binary or proportion responses. - `Gamma` — log link, `V(mu) = mu^2`; for positive, right-skewed continuous data. - `NegativeBinomial` — log link, `V(mu) = mu + mu^2/theta`; for overdispersed counts. - `Beta` — logit link; for proportions strictly between 0 and 1. - `Tweedie` / `TweedieEstimated` (via `tw()`) — log link, `V(mu) = mu^p`; for compound Poisson-Gamma data with a point mass at zero (e.g. insurance claims). - `InverseGaussian` — log link, `V(mu) = mu^3`; for positive, heavy-tailed continuous data. - `CoxPH` — proportional hazards partial likelihood; for survival/time-to-event data. - `OrderedCategorical` — cumulative logit (proportional odds); for ordinal responses. - `Multinomial` — baseline-category logit; for unordered categorical responses. - `QuantileFamily` — Extended Log-F (ELF) smooth pinball loss; for quantile regression. For distributional regression, where more than one parameter of the response distribution (e.g. both the mean and the scale) is modeled by its own smooth predictor, see `GAMLSSFamily` and its concrete subclasses (`GaussianLS`, `GammaLS`, `BetaLS`, `ZeroInflatedPoisson`, `ZeroInflatedNegativeBinomial`). ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Families are passed to `GAM` via the `family` argument; they are rarely instantiated by users beyond that. ::: {#92d96046 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import whittaker as wk rng = np.random.default_rng(0) n = 200 x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n) y = rng.poisson(np.exp(0.5 * np.sin(x))) data = {"x": x, "y": y} # Any concrete Family subclass can be passed to GAM model = wk.GAM("y ~ s(x)", family=wk.Poisson()) model.fit(data, method="REML") print(model.summary()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` GAM fit summary ============================================================ Formula: y ~ s(x) Family: Poisson(link='log') Observations: 200 Coefficients: 10 Parametric coefficients: Term Estimate Std.Err z value p-value ------------------------ ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------- (Intercept) 0.2113 0.0657 3.214 0.00131 Approximate significance of smooth terms: Term EDF Ref.df Chi.sq p-value ------------------------ ------ ------ ---------- ---------- s(x) 4.18 5 37.260 5.312e-07 Total EDF: 5.18 Deviance: 187.0851 Null dev: 230.5815 Dev. expl: 18.9% GCV score: 0.985797 Scale est: 1.000000 AIC: 554.30 BIC: 571.37 ``` ::: ::: ## Attributes {.doc-attributes}
Name Description
scale_known Whether the dispersion (scale) parameter is fixed rather than estimated.
### [scale_known]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} Whether the dispersion (scale) parameter is fixed rather than estimated. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [scale_known]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} Returns `True` for families with no free dispersion parameter (e.g. `Binomial`, `Poisson`), in which case the scale is always `1` and is not estimated during fitting. Returns `False` (the default) for families such as `Gaussian` and `Gamma`, whose scale is estimated from the data. ::: ## Methods {.doc-methods}
Name Description
deviance() Total (unscaled) deviance.
initialize() Compute starting values for `mu` given the observed response `y`.
irls_update() Custom IRLS pseudo-response and working weights.
link() Apply the link function $g(\mu)$, mapping the conditional mean to the linear predictor.
link_derivative() Derivative of the link function, $g'(\mu) = d\eta/d\mu$.
link_inverse() Apply the inverse link $g^{-1}(\eta)$, mapping the linear predictor back to the mean.
log_likelihood() Log-likelihood $\ell(y; \mu, \phi)$ evaluated at the given scale parameter $\phi$.
simulate() Simulate response values from the distribution.
unit_deviance() Per-observation deviance contributions $d_i$, before summing over observations.
variance() Variance function $V(\mu)$ relating the response variance to its mean.
### [deviance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Total (unscaled) deviance. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L164-L189){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python deviance(y, mu, *, weights=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} $D(y, \hat\mu) = 2 \sum_i [\ell(y_i; y_i) - \ell(y_i; \hat\mu_i)]$. The deviance measures the discrepancy between the fitted model and a saturated model that fits the data exactly. It is used by `GAM.fit()` for smoothing parameter selection (GCV) and by `GAM.summary()` for goodness-of-fit reporting. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values, shape `(n,)`. [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fitted conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional prior weights, shape `(n,)`. When given, the deviance is $\sum_i w_i d_i$ rather than $\sum_i d_i$. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The total deviance. ::: ### [initialize()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Compute starting values for `mu` given the observed response `y`. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L299-L318){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python initialize(y) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Called once before the first P-IRLS iteration to seed the mean. The default implementation returns `y` unchanged, which is appropriate for the `Gaussian` family with its identity link. Families with non-identity links or constrained means (e.g. `Poisson`, `Binomial`, `Gamma`) override this to nudge `y` into the valid range and avoid numerical issues (such as `log(0)`) on the first iteration. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Starting values for `mu`, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [irls_update()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Custom IRLS pseudo-response and working weights. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L271-L297){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python irls_update(y, mu, eta) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Override in families whose loss does not fit the standard GLM deviance framework (e.g. `QuantileFamily`, `CoxPH`, `OrderedCategorical`, `Multinomial`), to supply the working response `z` and working weights `W` directly rather than deriving them from `link`, `link_derivative`, and `variance`. Returning `None` (the default) tells the P-IRLS loop to fall back to the standard GLM formula `z = eta + (y - mu) * link_derivative(mu)`, `W = 1 / (link_derivative(mu)^2 * variance(mu))`. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values, shape `(n,)`. [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Current fitted mean values, shape `(n,)`. [eta]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Current linear predictor values, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple of NDArray, or None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `(z, W)`, the pseudo-response and diagonal working-weight vector, each shape `(n,)`, or `None` to use the default GLM formula. ::: ### [link()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Apply the link function $g(\mu)$, mapping the conditional mean to the linear predictor. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L82-L102){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python link(mu) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The link function defines the relationship $\eta = g(\mu)$ between the mean of the response and the linear predictor. Each family provides a canonical or default link; for example, the identity link for Gaussian, the log link for Poisson, and the logit link for Binomial. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Conditional mean values $\mu$, shape `(n,)`. Must lie in the valid range for the family (e.g., $\mu > 0$ for Poisson, $0 < \mu < 1$ for Binomial). ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Linear predictor values $\eta = g(\mu)$, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [link_derivative()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Derivative of the link function, $g'(\mu) = d\eta/d\mu$. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L123-L141){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python link_derivative(mu) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Used by the P-IRLS fitting loop to form the working response `z` and working weights `W` at each iteration, via a first-order (delta-method) linearization of the link function around the current fit. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Conditional mean values $\mu$, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Derivative values $g'(\mu)$, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [link_inverse()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Apply the inverse link $g^{-1}(\eta)$, mapping the linear predictor back to the mean. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L104-L121){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python link_inverse(eta) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} This is the transformation applied to the fitted linear predictor to recover fitted values `mu` on the response scale, e.g. after `GAM.predict()` computes `eta`. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [eta]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Linear predictor values $\eta$, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Conditional mean values $\mu = g^{-1}(\eta)$, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [log_likelihood()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Log-likelihood $\ell(y; \mu, \phi)$ evaluated at the given scale parameter $\phi$. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L212-L238){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python log_likelihood(y, mu, scale, *, weights=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Used by `GAM.fit()` for REML/ML-based smoothing parameter selection and by `GAM.summary()` for reporting AIC and related fit statistics. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values, shape `(n,)`. [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fitted conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. [scale]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dispersion (scale) parameter $\phi$. [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional prior weights, shape `(n,)`. When given, the log-likelihood is $\sum_i w_i \ell_i$ rather than $\sum_i \ell_i$. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The total log-likelihood. ::: ### [simulate()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Simulate response values from the distribution. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L251-L269){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python simulate(mu, scale, rng) ``` ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Mean (fitted values), shape `(n,)`. [scale]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Estimated scale parameter φ. [rng]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [np.random.Generator]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A `numpy.random.Generator` instance. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Simulated response values, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [unit_deviance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Per-observation deviance contributions $d_i$, before summing over observations. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L191-L210){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python unit_deviance(y, mu) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The total deviance returned by `deviance` is $\sum_i d_i$ (or the weighted sum). The default implementation here is `(y - mu)^2`, appropriate for the Gaussian family; concrete families with a different deviance formula override this method. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values, shape `(n,)`. [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fitted conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Per-observation deviance contributions $d_i$, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [variance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Variance function $V(\mu)$ relating the response variance to its mean. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/fix-oom-problems/whittaker/families/base.py#L143-L162){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python variance(mu) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The conditional variance of the response is $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \phi \, V(\mu)$, where $\phi$ is the dispersion (scale) parameter. For the Gaussian family this is constant (`1`); for Poisson it is `mu`; for Gamma it is `mu^2`, etc. `variance` is used by P-IRLS to form the working weights. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Conditional mean values $\mu$, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Variance function values $V(\mu)$, shape `(n,)`. :::
